tips: Don't give up in the genealogies (chapters 1–9). They were written for exiles returning home who needed to know they still belonged to Israel's story, which reaches back to Adam.
Compare it with 2 Samuel. Chronicles retells David's reign but leaves out his sin with Bathsheba and focuses on his preparations for the temple and its worship.
Read it as a message of hope for a small, discouraged community: God's promises to David and his care for true worship still stand.

looksBack.title: Retelling Samuel and Kings
looksBack.text: Much of Chronicles parallels the earlier histories; for example, God's covenant with David in 1 Chronicles 17 retells 2 Samuel 7.

looksAhead.title: The temple Solomon will build
looksAhead.text: David gathers materials and organizes the priests and singers (1 Chronicles 22–29) for the temple that Solomon builds in 2 Chronicles 3–7.

looksAhead.title: Genealogies and Jesus
looksAhead.text: Matthew opens his Gospel with a genealogy that follows the same line from Abraham through David (Matthew 1:1–16; 1 Chronicles 1–3).

tips: Notice that Chronicles follows only the kings of Judah. The northern kingdom appears only where it touches Judah, because the writer's focus is David's line and the temple in Jerusalem.
Look for the key promise in 2 Chronicles 7:14: if God's people humble themselves, pray, and turn from their wicked ways, he will hear and heal. Each king's story tests it.
Pay special attention to the reforms of Hezekiah (chapters 29–32) and Josiah (34–35). Chronicles gives them far more space than Kings does.

looksBack.title: David's preparations
looksBack.text: Solomon builds the temple his father planned (1 Chronicles 28:11–21), and the fire and glory that fill it (2 Chronicles 7:1–3) recall the tabernacle in Exodus 40:34–35.

looksAhead.title: Cyrus and the return
looksAhead.text: The book ends with Cyrus allowing the exiles to go home (2 Chronicles 36:22–23), the same words that begin Ezra (Ezra 1:1–3).

looksAhead.title: The last book of the Hebrew Bible
looksAhead.text: In the Hebrew ordering, Chronicles comes last, so the Old Testament ends on the invitation to go up and rebuild.

tips: Notice the gap between chapters 6 and 7: about fifty-seven years pass. Chapters 1–6 tell of the first return and the rebuilding of the temple; chapters 7–10 tell of Ezra's own mission to teach the law.
Watch how often the book credits God for moving foreign kings—Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes. The repeated phrase "the hand of the LORD his God upon him" (Ezra 7:6) shows who is really in control.
Read Ezra's prayer of confession (chapter 9) as the book's spiritual center. The problem of intermarriage with idolaters threatens the community's identity as God's people.

looksBack.title: The prophecy of seventy years
looksBack.text: The return comes "that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled" (Ezra 1:1), referring to Jeremiah's promise in Jeremiah 29:10.

looksAhead.title: Haggai and Zechariah
looksAhead.text: When the temple rebuilding stalls, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah urge the people on (Ezra 5:1; 6:14); their messages are recorded in the books named after them.

looksAhead.title: Rebuilding the walls
looksAhead.text: Nehemiah continues the story about thirteen years after Ezra arrives, turning from the temple to the walls of Jerusalem.

tips: Read it as a leader's journal. Much of it is in Nehemiah's own voice, including short prayers in the middle of action (Nehemiah 2:4; 4:4–5; 13:31).

Notice that the wall is finished in only fifty-two days (Nehemiah 6:15), yet the book keeps going. The real goal is not a wall but a renewed people, which is why the reading of the law follows (chapter 8).
Don't skip the sad ending (chapter 13). Within a few years the people break the promises they made, showing that rebuilding walls cannot change hearts.

looksBack.title: Ezra's mission
looksBack.text: Ezra reappears in Nehemiah 8, reading the law to the people, continuing the work begun in Ezra 7–10.

looksAhead.title: Malachi's complaints
looksAhead.text: The problems Nehemiah confronts—neglected tithes, careless priests, and marriages to idolaters (Nehemiah 13)—are the same ones Malachi addresses (Malachi 1:6–8; 2:11; 3:8–10).

looksAhead.title: The end of Old Testament history
looksAhead.text: Nehemiah is the last narrative of Israel's history in the Old Testament; about four centuries pass before the New Testament opens.

tips: Notice that God is never mentioned by name. Read for the "coincidences"—a sleepless king, a well-timed reading of the records (Esther 6:1–3)—and ask who is working behind them.
Watch for reversals. Haman builds a gallows for Mordecai and is hanged on it; a decree to destroy the Jews becomes a day of deliverance (Esther 9:1).
Read Mordecai's challenge to Esther as the turning point: "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (Esther 4:14).

looksBack.title: An old enemy
looksBack.text: Haman is called "the Agagite" (Esther 3:1), recalling Agag king of the Amalekites, Israel's ancient enemy whom Saul failed to destroy (1 Samuel 15:8–9). Mordecai, like Saul, is a Benjamite descended from Kish (Esther 2:5).

looksAhead.title: The feast of Purim
looksAhead.text: The book explains the origin of Purim (Esther 9:20–32), a festival Jewish communities still celebrate by reading Esther aloud.

looksAhead.title: God's people preserved
looksAhead.text: By preserving the Jewish people in exile, the story protects the line through which the promised Messiah would come.
